analysis.one_liner: Bars lenders from changing mortgage terms after application and requires early written disclosures with a three-day withdrawal right.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill died in a House Banking subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act so that a mortgage lender must honor the terms it originally disclosed to a borrower — it could not impose worse terms at closing, or make its offer expire on a countdown, unless it clearly warned the borrower the terms could change or the borrower caused an unreasonable delay [S2] [S3]. It would require lenders to mail or deliver full loan disclosures, itemizing fees like points, before the earlier of the loan closing or three days after receiving the application, and would let a borrower withdraw the application within three days of getting those disclosures without owing anything beyond reasonable handling fees [S2] [S3]. It also raises the civil penalty for failing to make the required mortgage disclosures from up to $1,000 to up to $10,000 [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers applying for mortgages gain protection from a common practice: lenders quoting attractive terms at application, then imposing costlier terms or a short expiration window at closing when the borrower has little leverage. Borrowers would get the full cost of the loan, including points and fees, in writing within three days, and could walk away without penalty if the numbers changed. Borrowers misled by missing disclosures would have ten times the damages to sue for.

how_it_helps.text: Lenders could not impose terms less favorable than those disclosed at application, nor make the disclosed offer expire on a countdown clock — the main exceptions being a clear warning that a term may change, or an unreasonable delay caused by the borrower [S2] [S3].

Full loan disclosures, including all lender fees in the finance charge (itemized), must be mailed or delivered before the earlier of loan closing or three days after the application is received [S2] [S3].
Borrowers get a three-day right to withdraw a written mortgage application after receiving the disclosures, owing only reasonable application-handling fees [S2] [S3].
The civil penalty for failing to make required mortgage disclosures rises from $100–$1,000 to $1,000–$10,000, giving borrowers a real remedy [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and creditors bear the cost of delivering disclosures earlier, itemizing all fees, honoring their quoted terms, and potentially paying tenfold larger penalties for disclosure failures. Lenders also lose the flexibility to reprice loans between application and closing, which in volatile rate environments they argue is a legitimate business need — though the bill carves out an exception when the disclosure clearly warns terms may change.

drawbacks.text: Locking lenders into originally disclosed terms removes the ability to reprice a mortgage when interest rates move between application and closing, which could make lenders charge more upfront or refuse to quote unless rates are locked for a fee — costs that flow back to borrowers [S3].

The bill does allow lenders to escape the lock-in simply by adding a clear statement that terms are subject to change, which a skeptical reader could see as a large loophole that limits the bill's practical bite [S2] [S3].
Higher penalties and earlier disclosure deadlines add compliance costs for lenders of all sizes, costs that smaller community lenders may find harder to absorb than large institutions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are real but modest: this is a disclosure-and-lock-in bill, not a rate cap or a ban on any lending practice, and the 'subject to change' exception lets lenders preserve much of the old flexibility by printing one clear sentence. The main value for borrowers is time and information — seeing the full cost, including fees, within three days, and being able to walk away without owing the loan. The main cost is lender compliance and some loss of repricing flexibility, which is likely passed to borrowers at the margin. On balance a fair trade, but not transformative.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee and then to its Consumer Affairs subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Dean Gallo (R-NJ) introduced the bill on January 20, 1989, with 14 Democrats and 5 other Republicans among its 19 cosponsors [S1] [S4].

The House referred it to the Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction, and on February 15, 1989, referred it to the Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs and Coinage [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and creditors are better off, because they never had to honor quoted terms, deliver disclosures within three days, itemize all fees, or face penalties up to $10,000 for missing disclosures. Homebuyers got none of the protections the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mortgage lenders, who avoided new rules

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 14 of 257 House Democrats and 5 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored, and neither party's leadership acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would force lenders to honor their originally disclosed mortgage terms, deliver itemized cost disclosures within three days, allow borrowers to withdraw without penalty, and face penalties up to $10,000 for missing disclosures. Stopping the bill preserved lenders' ability to reprice loans between application and closing and kept disclosure penalties low.
